summary: Formally defines Routing Backus-Naur Form, a variant of BNF already used by several routing area protocol specifications to describe message syntax. Sharing one defined notation makes related protocols easier to read and compare.

plainLanguage.summary: Engineers describe the shape of messages with a special shorthand. This note finally writes down the rules of that shorthand, so everyone reads the same message recipes the same way.

questions: what does ::= mean in rfc message syntax
subtitle: The written-down rules for the BNF dialect that RSVP, LMP and PCEP specifications already used to describe their messages.

tldr.problem: Several Routing Area protocols described their messages with a common variant of BNF, but nobody had ever formally defined that variant, which left room for confusion.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5511 names the variant Routing BNF (RBNF) and defines its rule names, its operators (assignment, concatenation, optional, alternative, repetition, grouping), its editorial conventions and its precedence order.
tldr.outcome: RBNF can be used to read existing RFCs and to write new extensions, mainly for protocols closely related to those that already use it. For wholly new, unrelated protocols the RFC says to consider a broader form such as ABNF.

today: RFC 5511 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the formal definition of RBNF as the RFC states it.

sections.title: Why RBNF Was Written Down
sections.content:
Backus-Naur Form (BNF) has been used to specify the message formats of several protocols in the IETF Routing Area. Those specifications were not based on any formal definition of BNF, and they differ slightly from definitions found elsewhere.

The RFC could have converted every old document to an established form such as ABNF (RFC 5234). It points out that this would be a lot of work, and that ABNF terminals are integers (characters or bytes), whereas here the terminals are objects (message elements) or entire messages. So conversion would also need extensions to ABNF.

Instead, the RFC defines the variant that is already in use, which it describes as similar to a subset of Extended BNF, and names it Routing BNF (RBNF). A written definition also makes automated verification of future documents possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a club that always wrote its recipes in a secret shorthand but never explained it. Rewriting every recipe would take forever, so they just wrote down the shorthand rules instead.

sections.title: Where RBNF Is Used and Where It Should Be
sections.content:
The first notable use of this BNF variant was in the specification of RSVP (RFC 2205). It then carried through RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) and the GMPLS signaling extensions (RFC 3473), each of which has produced many extension documents. The Link Management Protocol (RFC 4204) and the Path Computation Element Protocol (RFC 5440) use it too.

The applicability statement says RBNF should be used when writing extensions to those protocols, and may be used to interpret the older RFCs. It could also suit new protocols that are closely related to them. PCEP is the example: it is closely related to RSVP-TE, so its working group chose the same BNF form.

For a wholly new protocol unrelated to any that uses RBNF, the working group should consider carefully whether to use RBNF or a more formally specified, broader form such as ABNF. Using RBNF to extend protocols that use some other BNF form is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the shorthand when you are adding to a recipe book that already uses it. If you are starting a brand new book, think hard about using a more common shorthand instead.

sections.title: Rules, Objects, Constructs and Messages
sections.content:
An RBNF specification is a sequence of rule definitions. A rule is either a basic protocol object, usually drawn as a bit diagram in the protocol specification, or something built from other rules with operators. The order in which rules are defined does not matter, and definitions are read left to right on a line and top to bottom on the page.

Rule names are enclosed in angle brackets, as in <Path Message>. They may contain any printable characters but MUST NOT contain tabs or line breaks. No meaning should be read into the characters of a name. There are three kinds of rule, distinguished by naming habit:

  • Objects are the indivisible rules, typically named in uppercase with underbars, such as <SENDER_TEMPLATE>.
  • Constructs are built from other rules, named in lowercase with spaces or hyphens, such as <sender descriptor>.
  • Messages are the final goal, built from objects and constructs. The only syntactic difference from a construct is that no other rule is typically built from a message. They are usually in title case.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of LEGO. Single bricks are objects, small models made of bricks are constructs, and the finished set on the box is the message.

sections.title: The Operators
sections.content:
RBNF has six operators.

  • Assignment is written ::=. The left-hand side and the operator MUST be on the same line.
  • Concatenation is a sequence of objects and constructs, usually separated by spaces. They MUST appear in the order given.
  • Optional presence uses square brackets. Everything inside one pair of brackets is treated as a unit, so all of it is included or none of it, unless brackets are nested. In <construct> ::= <MAND> [ <OPT_1> [ <OPT_2> ] ], OPT_2 can only appear if OPT_1 does.
  • Alternatives use the pipe |: one rule or the other MUST be present.
  • Repetition uses three dots ... and means the preceding item MAY repeat. Combined with square brackets it gives zero or more.
  • Grouping uses round brackets to treat several items together. It is not mandatory but is RECOMMENDED for clarity.

Anything not marked optional is mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: The operators are the little signs in the recipe: this then that, maybe add this, pick one of these, repeat this as often as you like, and brackets to say which things go together.

sections.title: Conventions, Precedence and Ambiguity
sections.content:
White space and line breaks within an assignment are ignored but SHOULD be used for readability. A line break MUST NOT separate the left-hand side from ::=, and a new assignment MUST begin on a new line. Ordering is explicit, although a protocol specification MAY say that ordering is only RECOMMENDED, in which case elements MAY arrive in any order.

The RFC calls precedence the main opportunity for confusion. From tightest to loosest binding the order is: objects and constructs; repetition; grouping and optional; concatenation; alternative. So concatenation binds tighter than the pipe.

This matters for an old definition in RFC 2205 of <flow descriptor list>, which reads as an empty list or the list followed by a descriptor (formulation a), and not as the alternative reading (b). Implicit grouping by line breaks is common in older text but SHOULD be avoided in new definitions.

In new documents, multi-alternates such as <ALT_A> <ALT_B> | <ALT_C> <ALT_D> are not allowed. Explicit grouping or an intermediary construct MUST be used. Automated readers are REQUIRED to parse rules correctly with or without grouping, and must handle existing RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: If a recipe is worded in a way that two cooks might read differently, add brackets to make it clear. The note also says which reading wins if someone forgot the brackets.

sections.title: Validation Tools and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says RBNF would be appropriate for automated validation tools. Such tools would need to check close conformance to these rules for new documents, but should also parse RBNF as used in existing RFCs. At the time of writing, no tools were known.

The security section says the document defines no network behavior and does not introduce or try to solve any security issue. It notes that clear and unambiguous protocol specifications reduce the likelihood of incompatible or defective implementations that might be exploited in attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A notation does not send anything over the network, so it cannot be attacked directly. But clear instructions mean fewer mistakes when people build things from them.

items.label: Assignment
items.desc: Left-hand side is defined as the right-hand side.

items.label: Concatenation
items.desc: Items MUST appear in the order given.

items.label: Optional
items.desc: Contents may be present or absent; brackets can nest.

items.label: Alternative
items.desc: One rule or the other MUST be present.

items.label: Grouping
items.desc: Treat the contents together; RECOMMENDED for clarity.
